Yes. And your example is an interesting case because the **LaTeX source isn't itself an image**. It is a description of how to *generate* the image.

There are several normal workflows:

### 1. Compile the LaTeX document — the standard approach

The usual tools are:

- **TeX Live** — common on macOS/Linux
- **MiKTeX** — common on Windows
- **MacTeX** — the easiest full TeX distribution for macOS
- **Overleaf** — browser-based LaTeX environment

You put the figure inside a `.tex` document and compile it, normally producing a **PDF**. LaTeX graphics packages such as TikZ and PGF can generate vector graphics directly during compilation.  ([Overleaf](https://www.overleaf.com/learn/latex/Pgfplots_package?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

For example:

```latex
\documentclass{article}
\usepackage{graphicx}

\begin{document}

% your figure here

\end{document}
```

Then:

```text
pdflatex document.tex
```

and you view `document.pdf` in Preview, Acrobat, Skim, etc.

---

### 2. Use Overleaf

For someone who doesn't want to install a TeX system, **Overleaf** is probably the easiest approach.

You paste the LaTeX source into an Overleaf project and press **Compile**. The resulting PDF is displayed in the browser. Overleaf supports TikZ/PGF-generated graphics as well as ordinary image files.  ([Overleaf](https://www.overleaf.com/learn/latex/Inserting_Images?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

[Overleaf LaTeX editor](https://www.overleaf.com/)

---

### 3. Generate the figure as a separate PDF

For graphics made with TikZ, PGFPlots, etc., a particularly useful workflow is **externalization**.

The LaTeX system compiles the graphic and saves it as a separate PDF:

```text
diagram.tex
     ↓
LaTeX
     ↓
diagram.pdf
```

The PDF is a genuine vector graphic, so you can view it independently or subsequently include it in another document. TikZ's `external` library is specifically designed for this.  ([Overleaf](https://www.overleaf.com/learn/latex/Questions%2FI_have_a_lot_of_tikz%2C_matlab2tikz_or_pgfplots_figures%2C_so_I%27m_getting_a_compilation_timeout._Can_I_externalise_my_figures%3F?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

This is especially useful for a large collection of diagrams.

---

### 4. In your particular example: `.PS` means something different

This is the important part.

Your code contains:

```text
.PS
...
.PE
```

and commands such as:

```text
box "sum"
line
spline from X.s ...
```

That is **not TikZ**.

It is **PIC** language — specifically the Unix/AT&T `pic` diagram language — embedded inside a LaTeX document. The `\box\graph` construction is associated with a traditional `pic`/troff workflow.

So your historical source is actually closer to:

```text
LaTeX
  │
  └── embedded PIC program
          │
          ▼
        pic
          │
          ▼
   diagram/graphics
          │
          ▼
       LaTeX
          │
          ▼
         PDF
```

That's why simply giving the source to a modern TikZ-oriented LaTeX renderer isn't necessarily going to reproduce the original figure.

### If you're trying to reproduce this *specific historical figure*

I'd actually recommend **not converting it to TikZ immediately**.

We could investigate the original **PIC → LaTeX** toolchain and determine exactly what `\box\graph`, `.PS`, `.PE`, `spline`, `move to`, etc. were intended to run through. That could potentially let us reproduce the diagram **faithfully from the original source**, rather than having an AI redraw it approximately—as happened with the image I generated above.

That distinction could be particularly important for your work with older computer-science documents and software history.

For this specific PIC figure

- Reproduce it with the original PIC toolchain

Yes. If the goal is **legacy-document preservation + high-definition fragment addressability + decentralized distribution**, I would build something considerably more structured than a conventional “LaTeX → PDF/HTML” converter.

The architecture I would recommend is:

```text
                 ORIGINAL ARTIFACT
                       │
          ┌────────────┴────────────┐
          │                         │
     .tex source                assets/fonts
          │
          ▼
     LaTeXML parser
          │
          ▼
   semantic XML representation
          │
     ┌────┴─────────┐
     │              │
  text/math       PIC blocks
     │              │
     │           GNU pic / dpic
     │              │
     │              ▼
     │             SVG
     │              │
     └──────┬───────┘
            ▼
       enriched HTML/XML
            │
     ┌──────┼─────────────┐
     │      │             │
     ▼      ▼             ▼
   HTML   SVG/MathML    metadata
     │      │             │
     └──────┼─────────────┘
            ▼
       fragment graph
            │
            ▼
       Merkle / CID DAG
            │
            ▼
     IPFS / other networks
```

The important conceptual shift is this:

> **The document should become a graph of addressable things, rather than a file that happens to contain things.**

### 1. LaTeXML should be the first major tool

I would make **LaTeXML** the principal LaTeX conversion engine.

It was specifically designed to transform TeX/LaTeX into XML and subsequently HTML, MathML, EPUB, JATS, etc. More importantly for your purpose, its intermediate XML representation retains document structure and identifiers rather than simply producing a visual rendering.  ([GitHub](https://github.com/brucemiller/latexml?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

For example:

```latex
\section{The Sumdiff Routine}
\label{sumdiff}

The routine computes ...

\begin{figure}
   ...
\end{figure}
```

could become something conceptually like:

```xml
<section xml:id="sumdiff">
  <title>The Sumdiff Routine</title>

  <p xml:id="sumdiff.p1">
     The routine computes ...
  </p>

  <figure xml:id="sumdiff.fig1">
     ...
  </figure>
</section>
```

That gives you a **semantic tree** instead of a page image.

LaTeXML itself explicitly supports assigning identifiers and building interconnected collections of documents. Its documentation even describes prefixing identifiers across documents so that every targetable element has a unique identifier.  ([GitHub](https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/blob/master/doc/manual/manual.tex?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That's remarkably close to what you're envisioning.

---

## 2. Treat PIC as a first-class language, not as an image

This is the part I would emphasize particularly strongly for your project.

Your `.PS ... .PE` material should **not be rasterized**.

The legacy PIC source is valuable information.

For example:

```text
SUM: box "sum"
DIFF: box "diff"
SH: box "sumdiff"
```

contains knowledge that a PNG doesn't:

```text
SUM
  type = box
  label = "sum"

DIFF
  type = box
  label = "diff"

SH
  type = box
  label = "sumdiff"
```

I would therefore preserve **three representations**:

```text
original PIC source
       │
       ├── canonical PIC
       │
       ├── SVG representation
       │
       └── semantic graph representation
```

### Use `dpic`

**dpic** is particularly interesting here.

It accepts PIC and can emit:

- SVG
- TikZ/PGF
- PostScript
- PDF
- LaTeX
- MetaPost
- XFig

among others.  ([Ubuntu Manpages](https://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/trusty/man1/dpic.1.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

For your project I would primarily use:

```text
PIC → SVG
```

rather than:

```text
PIC → PDF → PNG
```

because SVG gives you a **vector document whose individual objects can themselves have identities**.

That is a huge advantage for your "high-definition addressability" idea.

---

# 3. SVG becomes the natural representation of a PIC diagram

Suppose your diagram contains:

```text
sum → diff → sumdiff
```

Instead of producing an opaque image:

```html
<img src="figure1.png">
```

you can produce something conceptually like:

```xml
<svg id="fig1">

  <g id="fig1.sum">
     <rect .../>
     <text>sum</text>
  </g>

  <g id="fig1.diff">
     <rect .../>
     <text>diff</text>
  </g>

  <g id="fig1.sumdiff">
     <rect .../>
     <text>sumdiff</text>
  </g>

  <g id="fig1.edge1">
     <path .../>
  </g>

</svg>
```

Now you have something extraordinary compared with a PDF or PNG:

```text
document
   └── figure
        ├── sum
        ├── diff
        ├── sumdiff
        ├── x
        ├── y
        ├── plus
        ├── minus
        └── connecting lines
```

Each of those can potentially become independently addressable.

And because SVG is XML, this meshes beautifully with the XML representation produced by LaTeXML.

---

# 4. I would use Web Annotations for fragment relationships

This is where **W3C Web Annotation** becomes very interesting.

The Web Annotation model explicitly supports annotations whose targets are **specific segments of a resource**, rather than only whole resources. It provides selectors for identifying portions of text, images, and other resources.  ([W3C](https://www.w3.org/TR/annotation-model/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

So instead of saying:

```text
This comment belongs to Figure 7.
```

you could say:

```text
This comment refers specifically to
Figure 7 → node "sumdiff" → text "sumdiff".
```

Conceptually:

```json
{
  "type": "Annotation",

  "body": {
    "type": "Comment",
    "value": "This is the routine being discussed."
  },

  "target": {
    "source": "CID-of-figure",
    "selector": {
       "type": "FragmentSelector",
       "value": "fig7.sumdiff"
    }
  }
}
```

That gives you a **distributed annotation layer** without requiring the annotation to be stored in the original document.

This is important.

The original artifact can remain immutable while an entirely different person, archive, or research project adds annotations.

---

# 5. IIIF is worth borrowing from—even if this isn't primarily an image project

I'd also look closely at **IIIF**.

IIIF's model has a very useful concept: a **Canvas** is an addressable coordinate space, and portions of that canvas can be separately identified. IIIF Presentation 3.0 explicitly supports spatial fragments using `xywh=` and Web Annotation selectors.  ([IIIF](https://iiif.io/api/presentation/3.0/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

This could give you a hierarchy such as:

```text
Document
   │
   ├── Page 17
   │     │
   │     ├── paragraph 17.3
   │     │
   │     └── Figure 17.1
   │            │
   │            ├── sum
   │            ├── diff
   │            └── sumdiff
   │
   └── Page 18
```

IIIF has already solved a substantial portion of the problem of **addressing parts of visual objects in distributed collections**.  ([IIIF](https://iiif.io/api/presentation/2.0/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

I'd therefore consider using IIIF concepts even if the ultimate objects are SVG rather than scanned pages.

---

# 6. TEI is another possible semantic layer

For your historical/computational-humanities work, I'd investigate **TEI XML** as well.

TEI gives essentially every element the possibility of an `xml:id`, and explicitly supports identifiers for segments of text.  ([Text Encoding Initiative](https://tei-c.org/release/doc/tei-p5-doc/en/html/ref-entry.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

You could therefore have:

```xml
<p xml:id="doc12.p47">
```

and:

```xml
<figure xml:id="doc12.fig3">
```

and potentially:

```xml
<figure xml:id="doc12.fig3">
    <graphic xml:id="doc12.fig3.svg"/>
</figure>
```

TEI is particularly attractive if this evolves into a **digital humanities archive** rather than simply a technical-document conversion system.

I wouldn't necessarily force every LaTeX document into TEI, though. **LaTeXML's native XML should probably remain the primary lossless intermediate representation**, with TEI as an optional scholarly encoding.

---

# 7. Then introduce content addressing

This is where your "decentralized network" requirement changes the architecture.

I'd use **IPFS/IPLD-style content addressing**.

An IPFS CID isn't a conventional URL. It is derived from the content's cryptographic hash and identifies the content independently of where it happens to be stored.  ([IPFS Docs](https://docs.ipfs.tech/concepts/content-addressing/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

So instead of:

```text
https://some-university.edu/archive/book.html#fig7
```

you could ultimately have something conceptually like:

```text
CID(document)
   │
   ├── CID(chapter)
   │
   ├── CID(paragraph)
   │
   ├── CID(figure)
   │     │
   │     ├── CID(sum)
   │     ├── CID(diff)
   │     └── CID(sumdiff)
   │
   └── CID(bibliography)
```

That's a **Merkle DAG**.

IPFS's documentation specifically describes collections and directories as DAG structures in which a CID can represent a subtree, while individual components can have their own content identifiers.  ([IPFS Docs](https://docs.ipfs.tech/how-to/content-addressing-data-sets/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That is extremely close to the architecture you're describing.

---

# 8. But don't use CIDs alone

There is an important subtlety.

I'd distinguish:

### Semantic address

```text
urn:example:doc123:fig7.sumdiff
```

meaning:

> "the sumdiff object in Figure 7 of document 123"

from:

### Content address

```text
bafy...
```

meaning:

> "this exact immutable byte/object."

You want **both**.

For example:

```text
semantic ID:
doc123.fig7.sumdiff

        ↓ resolves through manifest

CID:
bafybeih....
```

Why?

Because if you change the diagram, its CID changes. That's exactly what content addressing is supposed to do. But you don't want the *conceptual identity* of the object to disappear merely because somebody corrected a typo.

So I'd maintain:

```text
persistent logical identifier
              +
version identifier
              +
content identifier
```

---

# 9. The resulting "document" becomes a graph

This is the architecture I'd ultimately aim for:

```text
                         WORK
                          │
                 ┌────────┴────────┐
                 │                 │
             VERSION 1         VERSION 2
                 │                 │
             CID: A             CID: B
                 │
       ┌─────────┼─────────┐
       │         │         │
    Section    Figure    Equation
       │         │
       │       CID:F
       │         │
       │    ┌────┼─────┐
       │    │    │     │
       │   sum  diff  sumdiff
       │         │
       │         CID:X
       │
       └──── references ───────► another document
```

Now a citation doesn't have to mean:

> "Go download this 20 MB PDF."

It could mean:

> "Retrieve this particular mathematical expression / paragraph / diagram node."

That is a much more powerful model for a future knowledge network.

---

# 10. The toolchain I'd actually choose

For a prototype, I'd use:

| Function | Tool |
|---|---|
| Legacy LaTeX interpretation | **LaTeXML** |
| PIC interpretation | **GNU pic / dpic** |
| PIC → vector graphic | **dpic → SVG** |
| XML transformation | **XSLT 3 / Saxon** |
| Semantic document | **LaTeXML XML** |
| Web presentation | **HTML5** |
| Mathematics | **MathML** |
| Diagrams | **SVG** |
| Fragment identity | **XML `id` / URI identifiers** |
| Distributed annotations | **W3C Web Annotation** |
| Image/page addressing | **IIIF concepts** |
| Linked metadata | **JSON-LD** |
| Content addressing | **IPFS/IPLD** |
| Validation | **XML Schema / Relax NG / Schematron** |
| Version control | **Git** |
| Long-term source archive | original `.tex`, `.pic`, fonts, macros, build environment |

## One particularly important rule

**Never throw away the original LaTeX/PIC.**

I'd make the archive contain something like:

```text
archive/
│
├── source/
│   ├── document.tex
│   ├── figures.pic
│   ├── macros.sty
│   └── bibliography.bib
│
├── semantic/
│   └── document.xml
│
├── presentation/
│   ├── document.html
│   ├── figure-01.svg
│   └── equations/
│
├── metadata/
│   ├── manifest.jsonld
│   └── annotations/
│
└── provenance/
    ├── build.json
    ├── tool-versions.json
    └── hashes.json
```

The **PDF then becomes one derived view**, not the master.
